This study introduces a method to calculate the tunneling time of a massive particle using a Larmor clock, where the clock's initial and final spin orientations are defined by specific projection operators. We demonstrate that the degree of spin flipping serves as a reliable indicator of tunneling duration, yielding results consistent with those derived from Landau-Zener time formulas. Notably, this approach reveals an inverse relationship between the mean Larmor vector spin and the mean square Larmor vector spin with the tunneling time: as one increases, the other must decrease. We also observe that the spin vector deviates most significantly from its mean direction during the moment of peak tunneling probability. Finally, we apply this framework to analyze tunneling times within a one-dimensional potential barrier, employing a semiclassical approximation alongside exact analytical solutions for a spin-1/2 particle subject to a constant magnetic field.

We have investigated the leading-twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave nonrelativistic mesons, specifically the $\rho$ and $f_2$ mesons. By utilizing the optical method, we derived the corresponding sum rules for the moments of these distribution functions. Additionally, we derived analytical expressions for the two leading corrections to them.

We investigate a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation to investigate nonlinear quantum gates. Our analysis focuses on the conditions necessary for executing quantum logic operations within this framework. We demonstrate that nonlinear quantum gates can be implemented using either time-dependent or time-independent potentials. Our study outlines the specific requirements for constructing both controlled-NOT and Feynman gates, which rely on adjustable interaction strengths between the two components.

This work examines the relationship between BMS algebras and double soft graviton theorem, demonstrating that every double soft theorem can be formulated as a Fock space representation of a specific extension of the BMS symmetry. Furthermore, we establish that a universal subleading term exists within all double soft gravitational scattering amplitudes.

Current deep learning research predominantly focuses on training models from scratch or utilizing full fine-tuning, both of which are computationally expensive and hinder real-world deployment. This paper introduces an innovative approach to online ensemble continual learning that leverages a search space of compact neural architectures. By employing a reinforcement learning agent to select optimal structures within this space, the method achieves superior performance on continual learning benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, the system demonstrates an efficient balance between training speed and model accuracy.

We introduce a new method for defining metrics on manifolds featuring generalized complex structures. Applying this method to elliptic generalized K\"{a}hler structures yields metrics that are compatible with said structures. Furthermore, we present a specific construction method for creating Riemannian metrics on a given complex manifold. Utilizing this method, we identify a new self-dual, Ricci-flat metric on $\mathbb{C}^2$ that is compatible with an almost complex structure exhibiting non-zero antiself-dual curvature.

This paper focuses on analyzing permutation polynomials and complete permutation polynomials over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$. We examine several polynomials in three variables to determine their status as complete mappings. Additionally, we introduce new examples of these polynomials and study the differential properties associated with them.

Intestinal parasites are a significant global health challenge, particularly in developing nations, where their detection relies on a labor-intensive and error-prone manual process. This study introduces a novel, automated approach for classifying intestinal parasites using a Deep Belief Network (DBN) trained on microscopic images. The methodology begins with the segmentation of these microscopic views to isolate parasite regions, followed by the generation of image patches. These patches serve as input for a DBN composed of three stacked Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), which are trained to distinguish between parasite and non-parasite areas. The results demonstrate that this automated framework achieves superior classification accuracy compared to traditional manual diagnosis methods.

This study examines a non-zero-sum investment and reinsurance game involving two competing insurers, where the insurers' surplus dynamics are governed by a regime-switching model incorporating diffusion and jumps. The objective for each insurer is to maximize the long-term expected discounted terminal wealth. Following the derivation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) partial differential equation (PDE) governing the value function, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the game's equilibrium. To address the high dimensionality of the resulting HJI PDEs, we introduce a deep learning-based deep residual method for their numerical approximation. We further validate the proposed method through simulations.

This study introduces a dual-stage filtering and control framework designed to enhance the smoothness and stability of quadcopter trajectories. The approach relies on a dual-stage architecture: a Genetic Filter (GF) first estimates the position and velocity, while a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller generates the necessary thrust commands. The integration of the GF allows the system to effectively mitigate the impact of sensor noise on the velocity estimation, thereby ensuring smoother flight operations. To validate this strategy, the research presents a comprehensive simulation analysis. The results demonstrate that the proposed dual-stage strategy outperforms the standard configuration, which typically relies on a conventional filter and PID controller.

This study investigates low-energy pion-nucleon interactions within the framework of QCD, utilizing the Feynman-Hellmann theorem to derive a fundamental relationship between the low-energy constants of the chiral Lagrangian and quark masses. By employing the large-$N_c$ limit of QCD, we establish that quark mass dependencies exhibit a linear behavior for the coefficients $C_{i_1 \dots i_{N_c}}$ in a chiral expansion involving $N_c$ pseudoscalar meson fields. This linear dependence is subsequently leveraged to determine the $\mathcal{O}(p^4)$ low-energy constants, yielding results that align with the predictions of standard chiral perturbation theory.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHN) serves as a general-purpose instrument for investigating proton-proton collisions at the LHC. CMS is designed to detect Higgs bosons and search for new physics beyond the Standard Model, with a specific capability to resolve individual tracks within particles' collision debris. This track resolution relies on the detector's innermost component: the Pixel Detector. Comprising three mechanical structures known as "pilot disks," this detector features a modular design that facilitates rapid upgrades. Following a significant technological advancement in 2015, the upgrade included replacing the pixel pilot disks with new versions engineered to withstand higher radiation doses. This article details the reconstruction software developed for these new, radiation-hardened disks.

This study employs machine learning to classify the morphologies of active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies within the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) Wide Survey. We selected 1,000 objects with redshifts $z<1$ and spectral signatures of AGN activity from the HSC Data Release 2 catalog. To prepare for classification, we extracted 1000 $\times$ 1000 pixel images centered on each AGN host from the survey data. We then trained a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to distinguish between these AGN hosts and typical galaxies, achieving a test accuracy of 99.99%. Subsequently, we utilized a ResNet-152 CNN to classify the majority and spiral structures of the AGN hosts, yielding a 79.99% test accuracy. We also examined the relationship between the fraction of galaxies exhibiting spiral morphology and the Eddington ratio, finding a negative correlation. This trend suggests that AGN feedback may be responsible for suppressing star formation and stripping away spiral structure.

Short-range correlations (SRC) in nuclei are defined by high-momentum nucleons that typically appear in small groups, or "clusters," within a nucleus. While existing data on these systems are limited to momentum distributions, this study presents the first predictions for their phase-space distributions. We employ the Green's function Monte Carlo method to calculate the wave functions of light nuclei, enabling the computation of moments up to the second order. Our results indicate that nucleons in SRC clusters are not randomly distributed but instead concentrate near the nuclear center. Furthermore, we predict that the probability of finding a nucleon within an SRC cluster increases with the nucleon's kinetic energy.

This study introduces a new symmetry tailored for complex-valued functions within deep learning, offering a theoretical framework to examine the symmetries of complex deep neural networks. We demonstrate that this newly proposed symmetry reduces the number of trainable parameters and improves model generalization. Additionally, we establish a methodology for constructing symmetric complex-valued convolutional neural networks. Finally, we present experimental results that validate the efficacy of these symmetric complex CNNs.

This work examines the evolution of the gluon density within the proton, specifically investigating the onset of saturation effects and the phenomenon of geometrical scaling. It outlines the theoretical framework governing gluon saturation and its manifestation in gluon structure functions, while also exploring how these dynamics influence the nuclear modification factor in heavy ion collisions.

We investigate the origins of alpha-element abundance variations in low-metallicity stars by analyzing a sample of 1,000 chemical evolution models. These models employ a stochastic, subgrid-scale approach to simulate the chemical enrichment of individual star-forming regions (SFRs), which are linked by a turbulent diffusion process. Our results indicate that while turbulent diffusion eventually homogenizes alpha-element abundances across the galaxy, the primary source of abundance scatter in low-metallicity environments is the intrinsic dispersion of alpha-element yields within SFRs. This yield dispersion arises from the stochastic nature of massive star formation and the inherent variations in stellar initial mass function (SIFS) between regions. Furthermore, we find that the amplitude of these yield dispersions is sensitive to the star formation history, peaking at a star formation to stellar mass ratio of approximately 1.0. Additionally, we demonstrate that the magnitude of alpha-element scatter is modulated by the initial conditions of the simulation, specifically the spatial distribution of star formation and the initial metallicity of the gas.

This paper introduces a new toolbox designed to evaluate the sensitivity of machine learning models, featuring three distinct methods: a global surrogate approach, a local perturbation strategy, and a permutation-based technique. We apply this toolkit to a model predicting financial literacy levels, demonstrating its utility in financial contexts. The findings reveal that the surrogate method offers the most comprehensive interpretability, while the permutation approach is the most efficient. Additionally, the permutation method uniquely allows for the isolation of feature interactions, a capability shared only with the surrogate approach.

This study introduces a Quantum SNeaking UUnsupervisedly Discovering Dynamics (SQUID) framework designed to leverage unsupervised quantum machine learning for the dynamics analysis of complex systems. By utilizing a specialized quantum circuit architecture, the framework extracts essential information regarding a system's evolution from unsupervised datasets. The approach is demonstrated through two distinct applications: first, the unsupervised learning of time scales within a quantum spin system, and second, the prediction of future states in a chaotic system, specifically the Lorenz attractor.

This paper investigates the geometry of warped product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds within the framework of almost contact manifolds. We prove that if such a submanifold consists of three components—warped, vertical, and horizontal—where the vertical and horizontal sections are non-trivial, it cannot exist as a pointwise slant warped product. The study further explores and establishes key characteristics of contact anti-invariant warped product submanifolds and those composed of warping, warpproduct, and vertical/horizontal spaces. Additionally, we establish specific properties for almost $C$-projectable and $C$-projectable warped product structures. Finally, we present several concrete examples to validate these theoretical findings.

We propose a novel framework for detecting low-energy nuclear recoils using defects in diamond, leveraging the distinct optical signatures of individual color centers. This approach, termed PALE-OCENE, offers superior sensitivity to low-energy nuclear events compared to existing methods. The strategy relies on monitoring defect-specific photoluminescence to isolate rare, low-energy recoil events from the overwhelming background of thermal noise. By analyzing the defect spectrum through machine learning, the system can distinguish between different target materials, such as xenon or argon gases, or various target materials like lead or gold. The framework is designed to be broadly applicable across a wide range of existing and future color center types. The paper outlines the theoretical foundations of PALE-OCENE, demonstrates its performance through simulations, and identifies the most promising color centers for implementation.

We investigate the dynamics of active colloidal dimers within active fluids characterized by spatially varying activity. Our findings indicate that these molecules develop a preferred orientation relative to local activity gradients, leading to anisotropic spatial distribution. Furthermore, the steady-state density of the molecules exhibits significant modulation along these activity gradients.

We investigate the low-energy excitations of fractional quantum Hall systems by analyzing low-energy spectral sum rules for the spin structure factor. These sum rules, derived from the static spin susceptibility, are calculated using a recently developed numerical technique that reconstructs spectral functions from the dynamical structure factor. Our analysis reveals the presence of multiple magnetoroton branches in these systems. Furthermore, we examine the influence of particle interactions on these sum rules and the resulting magnetoroton patterns.

This study investigates the clustering algorithm designed for epidemics on networks, which functions by repeatedly swapping edges to progressively separate infected and healthy nodes into distinct clusters. The work analyzes the algorithm's performance across three contexts: Monte Carlo simulations on random graphs, a deterministic framework utilizing random regular graphs, and a dynamic model where the infection spreads via a contact process on a network. The findings indicate that clustering efficacy is contingent upon the ratio of infection level to network connectivity, with optimal results achieved when clustering occurs near the epidemic threshold.

The presence of point-source artifacts, appearing as characteristic "X" shapes in CMB maps, is a significant concern for the Planck mission, as these can bias the detection of the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect. This study investigates the application of maximum likelihood (ML) pixel-based methods for creating CMB maps, demonstrating that the resulting map quality is highly dependent on the specific choice of pixel likelihood function. We show that an appropriately designed likelihood function can effectively eliminate these "X" artifacts. Furthermore, the paper provides a general framework for constructing such a likelihood function tailored to arbitrary point-source models.

We address reference ambiguity in language-guided, goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, where multiple valid references can correspond to a single intended target. This issue causes a policy to fail in navigating among various valid targets. To tackle this, we introduce an active referencing framework that enables an agent to query its instructor for clarification whenever ambiguity is detected. Additionally, we propose a curriculum that incrementally increases the density of references during training to mitigate the difficulty of learning active referencing. Experiments on a modified Pick-and-Place environment demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses prior approaches in handling references and successfully achieves goal coverage within 100% of the time.

Quantum process tomography is a fundamental technique for characterizing quantum devices, a method that has been extensively developed over the last two decades. In this work, we introduce a novel approach termed shadow process tomography, leveraging recent advancements in "shadow norms" to characterize channels. We demonstrate that this new method is highly efficient for channels possessing low shadow norms, a category that encompasses many significant examples. Furthermore, we establish that shadow process tomography is universally applicable, capable of recovering the complete process matrix for any arbitrary channel.

This paper establishes precise bounds relating to the Cheeger constant for convex domains in two dimensions. Our findings refine a recent result by Figalli and Pratsouri and align with a conjecture proposed by Figalli, Müller, and Pratsouri. Additionally, we present several related conjectures and open questions.

This study addresses the challenge of optimizing communication for UAVs in time-critical scenarios, such as delivering data from a ground device to a base station within a fixed duration. The objective is to maximize the throughput achieved by this transfer. The work introduces a joint optimization framework that simultaneously refines the flight path and the communication protocols, including power allocation and modulation schemes. The resulting non-convex problem is addressed via an iterative algorithm capable of generating a locally optimal solution. The proposed solution is benchmarked against standard approaches, specifically a straight-line UAV trajectory and a terrestrial relay operating under ideal line-of-sight conditions. Simulation results demonstrate that the optimized trajectory combined with joint communication design significantly outperforms these baseline methods.

We employ the renormalization group method to investigate the bilayer graphene system, specifically focusing on Coulomb interactions. Our analysis reveals that, irrespective of the screening conditions, the system remains stable against the emergence of charge or spin density wave phases. However, we observe that the system becomes unstable toward the formation of superconductivity.

The thermal evolution of the conformation of the endofullerene Sc2TbN@C80 was examined using a combination of scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), scanning Auger electron microscopy (SAEM), and density functional theory (DFT). The experiments revealed that at room temperature, Sc2TbN@C80 initially adopts a C5v conformation when adsorbed on an h-BN buffer layer atop a Ni(111) substrate. Upon heating to 300 K, the molecule undergoes a reversible phase transition to a D5h conformation. This process is driven by the molecule's increased mobility at elevated temperatures, which allows it to access a lower-energy D5h state.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, connecting billions of smart devices to the internet. These devices are characterized by their low power consumption, small physical dimensions, and limited computational capabilities. As security breaches targeting IoT devices become increasingly common, there is an urgent need to secure the data they transmit. However, imposing heavy encryption algorithms on these constrained devices often exceeds their processing limits, rendering them unsuitable for the task. This paper introduces a new encryption algorithm specifically designed to meet the limitations of low-power IoT devices. The proposed method leverages a lightweight substitution box and a streamlined permutation technique to enhance security while maintaining computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the algorithm offers superior security compared to existing solutions, with significantly faster execution times and lower power consumption.

Quantum state tomography is essential for verifying quantum computers and communication systems, yet the high cost of measurements often hinders its practical application. This study introduces an experiment design framework for adaptive Ramsey sequence measurements that leverages quantum state parameters to optimize the allocation of resources. By integrating this framework with a sequential Bayesian approach, the proposed method adaptively updates the experiment design with every new measurement. Simulation results demonstrate that this adaptive strategy significantly boosts tomography efficiency compared to non-adaptive techniques.

This study introduces a novel network centrality metric termed Gromov Centrality (GOC), which leverages the concept of triangle inequality excess (TIE) to quantify the extent to which a node deviates from geodesic paths. GOC is calculated by determining the average TIE across all triangles that include a specific node. The metric's efficacy is validated through its application to both synthetic networks and real-world datasets. The analysis reveals a strong positive correlation between GOC values and established centrality metrics, specifically betweenness and load, while also demonstrating that nodes with high GOC scores are more likely to exhibit functional roles, such as acting as hubs or mediating information flow.

This work introduces a new gravitational theory built on a simple postulate: the gravitational field is a manifestation of the inertia of a test mass within a curved spacetime. We have established a set of field equations that are both self-contained and a complete system. Notably, the theory is formulated to be valid only within an azimuthally symmetric coordinate system, a choice that streamlines the governing equations. We have derived the corresponding metric tensor components and formulated the geodesic equations to describe test particle trajectories. Furthermore, we have established the requisite geodesic deviation and field equations, and we have demonstrated that the theory successfully reproduces the correct Newtonian limit as well as the gravitational field generated by a point mass.

We present a classification of matrix pencil bundles under strict equivalence, defining each equivalence class by a normal form. This form comprises the direct sum of a specific pencil polynomial in indeterminate $t$ and a nilpotent pencil matrix. Additionally, we establish an algorithm to compute the strict canonical decomposition for any given bundle.

We present a geometric interpretation of topological T-duality for flat holomorphic line bundles over tori, extending this to cases involving first Chern classes that are not exact. Additionally, we establish that topological T-duality acts as a generalized Fourier-Mukai functor on the derived categories of these line-bundle equipped spaces. We also show that this functor induces an isometry between the respective twisted K-theory cohomology groups.

We present an algorithm capable of embedding minor-free graphs with treewidth $O(\log^{O(1)} n)$ into a tree structure while distorting distances by a factor of $O(\log^{O(1)} n)$, where the exponent depends on the graph class. This approach improves upon the previous best approximation of $O(n^{1/4})$ established by D\"{u}rr, M\"{u}nch, and Neumann (SODA 2019) for planar graphs and extends the result to a broader category of graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a method for embedding these minor-free graphs into a graph with treewidth $O(\log^{O(1)} n)$ and pathwidth $O(\log^{O(1)} n)$ with an $O(\log^{O(1)} n)$ distortion, achieving a more efficient runtime of $O(m \log^{O(1)} n)$. This represents a significant speedup over the prior best time complexity of $O(m \log^{O(1)} n \log \log n)$ by Neumann et al. (FOCS 2019).

This study establishes that for strongly monotone discrete-time dynamical systems with smooth mappings, prevalent trajectories exhibit long-term prevalence behavior. Specifically, it is shown that for systems where the mapping is $C^r$ with $r \geq 2$, there exists a full measure subset within the phase space such that every trajectory starting from this subset eventually enters the region of attraction of some non-empty compact invariant set. This finding extends previous work by Kolyada, Snoha, and Mañé, who demonstrated a similar result for non-empty compact invariant sets specifically arising from non-wandering points. The current proof relies on two primary components: the established fact that for strongly monotone systems, the set of non-wandering points is itself invariant, and the application of the "prevalent shadowing lemma" developed by the authors in a 2019 paper.

Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is a hybrid algorithm designed to determine the ground state energy of Hamiltonians, with applications ranging from quantum chemistry to materials science. Although the standard VQE typically employs an Ansatz composed of two-qubit gates, this study introduces a novel variant leveraging single-qubit gates for excitation. We demonstrate that this new variant remains effective in calculating Hamiltonian eigenvalues. Furthermore, we establish that this adaptive VQE variant offers a more efficient resource utilization by reducing the number of required quantum gates.

Deep generative models, such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), are typically trained using the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), which relies on maximizing the quality of the approximate posterior distribution over latent variables. This study examines a distinct optimization target: the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of these latent variables. We demonstrate that this objective yields a more robust training procedure for VAEs, resulting in higher-quality latent representations and improved image reconstruction fidelity. Furthermore, this approach is versatile and can be applied to other deep generative frameworks, including normalizing flows and autoregressive models.

This signal is modeled as a "stiff-amplified" relic from an early universe phase where the equation of state parameter was $w = 1$. Such a scenario amplifies the primordial spectrum by a factor of $10^{10}$ relative to the standard scale-invariant inflationary prediction. This study presents the inaugural high-resolution ALMA Atacama Compact Array (ACA) observations of comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) at a distance of 1.1 AU, utilizing the 12m antenna array to map the extended CO(2-1) emission. The survey employed a 12x12 arcmin field of view with 10" pixel resolution, revealing a compact core and extended wings in the spectral line profile. We modeled the core as a point source emitting at 1.1 km/s with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 0.16 km/s, while the extended wings were fitted with a Lorentzian profile centered at 1.11 km/s and an FWHM of 0.31 km/s. The wings' line broadening is attributed to the comet's outflow velocity, allowing us to estimate a CO(2-1) column density of $1.1 \times 10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$ and a total flux of $1.1 \times 10^{14}$ erg s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$. Furthermore, the observed extended wings align with a model of a distributed CS source, offering the first evidence for this phenomenon in a comet. This study introduces an unsupervised speech synthesis framework that is both straightforward and highly effective. We present a unified acoustic model capable of jointly handling speech generation and phoneme alignment, which serves as a foundational component for our approach. Additionally, we propose a novel unsupervised speech disarticulation metric that effectively guides acoustic modeling and significantly enhances speech generation quality. Experimental results on the TCD-SST0 database demonstrate that our method achieves generated audio with perceptual fidelity nearly equivalent to a speech autoencoder trained using teacher-forcing strategies.

This study explores a complex formulation of the holographic dark energy (DE) quintessence model, utilizing an energy density scaling of $\rho_{DE} = \Lambda^2$ and an equation of state parameter $\omega_{DE} = -1 + \frac{2}{3} \frac{1}{\xi^2}$, where $\xi$ represents the complex Hubble parameter defined as $\xi = \frac{1}{H}(\dot{H} + H^2)$. By applying the Tsallis DE framework, we derive the corresponding field equation. Our analysis reveals that the real component of the imaginary part of the DE field oscillates, mirroring the behavior of real holographic DE. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the derived cosmological dynamics are consistent with observational data.

Multi-objective optimization involves finding a solution set that optimizes multiple, often conflicting, goals. In this context, the Pareto front represents the collection of non-inferior solutions. However, standard single-objective methods struggle to address these multi-dimensional challenges effectively. While popular algorithms like NSGA-II have been widely adopted for multi-objective optimization, they face limitations when dealing with mixed-integer non-linear problems (MINLPs), particularly regarding constraint handling and local optima navigation. To overcome these hurdles, this paper introduces a novel branch-and-bound algorithm enhanced with NSGA-II. This hybrid approach leverages the global search capabilities of the evolutionary strategy to manage constraints and constraints violations, while integrating a dedicated local search within the branching logic to refine solutions and escape local traps. The proposed framework utilizes NSGA-II's sorting and crowding distance mechanisms to maintain diversity and manage the Pareto front. Empirical testing on a multi-objective MINLP benchmark demonstrates that the algorithm generates high-quality, well-distributed Pareto sets that are superior to those produced by the standalone NSGA-II.

We demonstrate within Synthetic Differential Geometry that internal connected Lie groupoids possess integral complete connected morphisms as a sufficient criterion for establishing internal connectedness.

The rapid expansion of biomedical datasets has created a critical need for secure, efficient sharing mechanisms to support collaborative research. To meet this demand, the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health are funding the development of the Biomedical Data Research Environment (BDRE), a dedicated cyberinfrastructure gateway designed for safe data exchange within the biomedical sector. This paper outlines the initial design principles and implementation progress of BDRE, with a specific focus on its security architecture.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to determine the sentiment polarity toward specific components within text. While deep learning models have achieved significant success in ABSA, they often struggle to capture implicit sentiments that are not explicitly stated. This study introduces iSPiP, a novel framework designed to enhance ABSM by learning implicit sentiment representations. The framework utilizes a Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (SCP) approach to generate sentiment-aware implicit sentiment embeddings. During the pre-training phase, the Supervised Contrastive (SC) loss function identifies and groups similar sentiment embeddings based on their supervision labels. Furthermore, the framework employs a sentiment-guided attention mechanism within a BERT-based sentiment classification model to enhance performance. Experimental results across three benchmark datasets indicate that iSPiP surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

Cases and controls are standard designs in epidemiological research, often used to investigate causal pathways where an exposure influences an outcome through an intermediate factor. This paper establishes identification conditions for direct and indirect effects in such case-control studies involving a binary mediator, using data from a randomized trial. We demonstrate that these effects are uniquely determined by the observed joint distribution of exposure, mediator, and disease status, contingent upon a positivity assumption and a specific independence condition regarding the mediator and exposure status within exposed subpopulations. Furthermore, we propose a flexible estimator based on weighted regression for calculating these effects, which remains valid even if the model assumptions are misspecified. Simulation results indicate that our method offers unbiased estimates with good statistical power, and we apply this approach to a prospective study examining the causal impact of alcohol consumption on stroke risk via blood pressure.

This study investigates secure multi-user transmission within an RIS-assisted system, accounting for hardware impairments (HIs) in both the transmitter and the RIS. The primary objective is to maximize the secure sum rate (SR) by optimizing RIS phase shifts and the transmitter's beamforming vectors, subject to total transmit power and unit norm constraints on the RIS phases. To address these HIs, the authors formulate a relaxed non-convex problem and solve it using an alternating optimization approach that combines semidefinite programming (SDP) with zero-forcing (ZF) techniques. Furthermore, a second approach is developed by relaxing the beamforming variables into matrix forms and applying majorization-minimization (MM) alongside SDP to achieve a near-optimal SR. Simulation results confirm that the proposed schemes outperform conventional methods lacking RIS assistance and systems ignoring HIs, demonstrating the effectiveness of the solutions.

This study introduces a novel contrastive value-based policy designed to enhance the core mechanisms of executive function within deep reinforcement learning (RL). By enabling an agent to dynamically sample and re-evaluate its past experiences, this approach optimizes learning efficiency. We specifically advance state-of-the-art performance by introducing a hindsight contrastive value (CV) method that leverages a dedicated summarizer to evaluate experiences. This summarizer contrasts the anticipated versus actual rewards and action values to generate a hindsight score. We demonstrate that this CV function can be integrated into both model-based and model-free RL architectures. Furthermore, we apply it to two key tasks: (1) a dynamic resampling strategy that selects high-scoring experiences for training updates, and (2) a dynamic database management system that removes low-scoring experiences to conserve memory. We validate these methods across various environments, including Atari games, MuJoCo locomotion tasks, and robotic manipulation, showing consistent improvements in both sample efficiency and performance.

The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) spacecraft is on a historic trajectory toward the Sun, with a record-breaking closest approach of 4.3 solar radii achieved in October 2018. This mission aims to investigate the mechanisms behind solar wind acceleration and coronal heating. A primary objective involves measuring the energy flux carried by the solar wind, which is essential for understanding these acceleration processes. This study analyzes PSP data from the first three orbital passes to determine the energy flux at these unprecedented distances. The findings indicate that the energy flux scales with radial distance ($r$) as $r^{-2.05}$, a relationship consistent with the inverse-square law expected for a spherically symmetric source. Additionally, the energy flux was found to be highly variable, fluctuating by a factor of 2.5 over approximately 10-minute intervals. These results suggest that the solar wind originates from a source that is not only spherically symmetric but also exhibits significant short-term variability.

We establish a concept of numerable noncommutative principal bundle defined by a locally compact group acting on a $C^*$-algebra. This framework generalizes both the classical result by Steenrod regarding locally trivial fiber bundles and Elliott's 1998 numerability condition for $C^*$-extensions. Our approach relies on the existence of a locally finite partition of unity consisting of locally group invariant functions. Under this setup, we demonstrate that the resulting bundle possesses a locally split projection and that its equivariant $K$-theory forms a finitely generated module over the $K$-theory of its base algebra.

Additionally, we demonstrate that it is consistent with ZFC that $a$ is strictly less than $d$, confirming that these ultrafilter-related cardinal characteristics can indeed be ordered differently than previously consistent under ZFC assumptions.

This study explores the optical properties of a $q$-deformed optomechanical system featuring a single deformed harmonic oscillator cavity mode interacting with two two-level atoms entering one after another via a $\mathcal{Q}$-deformation framework. The analysis examines how non-classicality and $q$-deformation influence the system's transparency and light propagation speed. Employing the Jaynes-Cummings model within a deformed environment, we calculate the eigenstates and Hamiltonian matrix elements. The results indicate that atomic configurations permit the emergence of Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (ET), while the influence of nonlinearity on ET characteristics is notably minimal. Furthermore, we investigate fast and slow light phenomena driven by atomic resonances and demonstrate that an increase in the $q$-deformation parameter correlates with enhanced transparency and a reduction in absorption. Additionally, we find that the velocity of light transmission is highly sensitive to the states of the two atoms and the degree of $q$-deformation.

This study introduces a neural network approach for solving both hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs). The proposed method employs cell-average unknowns within a neural network framework, offering a unified numerical scheme capable of addressing homogeneous and inhomogeneous hyperbolic PDEs alongside their parabolic counterparts. By leveraging the parabolic formulation to compute cell averages, a novel numerical technique emerges that yields stable and precise approximations for the associated hyperbolic PDEs. The method's accuracy and stability are substantiated through a von Neumann analysis and a Lax-Wendrolo theorem. Furthermore, a unique capability of this approach is its ability to handle initial and boundary conditions that are incompatible with standard formulations. Numerical experiments are presented to validate the method's efficacy and efficiency.

The LHC's 2015 ALICE (A Large Ion Collider Experiment) data collection period, known as Run 2, was a significant milestone for the world's largest hadron collider physics program. This run, characterized by a 5.02 TeV proton-proton center-of-mass energy and peak luminosities reaching 2.5 × 10²⁷ cm⁻² s⁻¹, enabled unprecedented studies of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) within heavy-ion collisions. In contrast, Run 3 will operate proton-proton collisions at a higher energy of 5.36 TeV with an anticipated luminosity of up to 2.5 × 10³⁴ cm⁻² s⁻¹, while also supporting high-energy heavy-ion collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.36 TeV per nucleon pair. To handle the significantly increased data rates and detector occupancy expected during these runs, ALICE has undergone a comprehensive upgrade. This upgrade includes a new inner tracking system, a high-granularity electromagnetic calorimeter, a high-performance muon arm, and a high-performance event trigger system. These upgrades have allowed ALICE to maintain its position as a leading experiment in heavy-ion physics, with a particular focus on studying the QGP in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.36 TeV per nucleon pair.

We investigate the relationship between the timelike Unruh effect and the Berry phase generated by an accelerating observer. Our analysis reveals that this geometric quantum phase arises from the entanglement between modes confined within future light cones and those within past light cones. This relationship offers a novel framework for investigating the timelike Unruh effect through the measurement of a geometric property.

Event extraction (EE) is a crucial task in information extraction that identifies events within text along with their associated arguments. Although significant advancements have been made in EE for English, progress in other languages remains limited. This paper introduces MEE, a multilingual dataset designed to advance research in this area. MEE comprises 10,000 annotated documents covering 10 languages and 1,000 event types per language. These annotations utilize the recently developed Multi-lingual Event Markup Language (ML-MEL). We also present MEE-Toolbox, a user-friendly tool that supports annotators in creating high-quality annotations. Experimental results indicate that utilizing MEE alongside MEE-Toolbox yields state-of-the-art performance across all ten languages.

This work introduces a positive universal vector bundle for every universal formal group law, generalizing the concept previously known only for universal formal group laws of even genus. Generalizing results by the author and Ravi Vakil regarding the relation between Chern classes and Todd classes within the context of the odd-genus formal group law, we derive an expression for push-forward operations involving these new bundles. Additionally, we demonstrate that the characteristic forms associated with our bundles are strictly positive.

This study investigates the impact of the stellar wind on the high-energy X-ray emission and variability of Cyg X-1 during its hard state. We analyzed data from the XMM-Newton mission, acquired during an observation in the 2012–2013 period, utilizing the X-ray emission model that incorporates a stellar wind component. Our results indicate that the stellar wind accounts for approximately 10% of the observed hard X-ray flux and roughly 10% of the measured hard X-ray timing variability.

We investigate Yang-Mills theories extended with a non-abelian aether-like term, demonstrating that this extension imposes stringent restrictions on the allowable structure of non-abelian vectors and tensors. Furthermore, by examining the high-temperature behavior of these theories, we derive the conditions necessary for the onset of spontaneous symmetry breaking.

This paper introduces a novel model that unifies syntactic parsing and semantic parsing by leveraging the shared dependency parse tree structure. Our approach utilizes a single, shared neural architecture to perform both operations simultaneously, significantly reducing the computational cost associated with running separate models. We evaluate this system against leading single-purpose parsers on standard datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Penn Treebank (PTB) for syntax and the CoNLL-UD dataset for semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our unified framework supports multiple languages, specifically English and German.

This study investigates magnetized outflows from neutrino-cooled accretion disks following the merger of compact objects. We utilize the GRMHD code to simulate a magnetorotational instability (MRI)-active, self-gravitating, and cooling accretion disk, which is initialized with a magnetic flux of $\Phi \sim 10^{27}$ G cm$^2$. The simulation reveals that the disk generates a magnetized outflow with a mass of $\sim 10^{-3} M_{\odot}$ and a kinetic energy of $\sim 10^{50}$ erg. This outflow originates from the outer regions of the disk, where the Shakura-Sunyaev $\alpha$-parameter is approximately 0.01, and is driven by magnetic buoyancy. The results indicate that such an outflow could significantly impact the r-process nucleosynthesis and the gravitational wave signal associated with kilonovae.

We investigate the merger history of massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) at redshifts $z \sim 1.5$ and $z \sim 2$ by analyzing their tidal structures using an extensive sample of 1,000 galaxies with $M_{\rm K} < -23$ mag drawn from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. By quantifying the flux fraction of tidal material, we find that $f_{\rm tidal} \sim 10\%$ for both redshift bins, a result consistent with lower redshift studies and independent of galaxy mass. This lack of evolution in tidal prevalence suggests that the merger rates of these massive ETGs remain constant over cosmic time, a conclusion supported by our estimated rate of $\sim 0.01$ per Gyr at $M_{\rm K} \sim -23$ mag. These findings align with the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, which predicts that most galaxy mergers occur at late times.

This study represents the second installment in a series exploring the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a theory grounded in the same foundational principles as General Relativity (GR) but formulated within a specific coordinate system. In this framework, GR's Laplacian is substituted with a Laplace-Beltrami operator. The resulting gravitational field equations are solved to determine the metric components, which subsequently yield expressions for the energy-momentum tensor and the gravitational field tensor. The analysis reveals that the theory predicts a repulsive gravitational field, a phenomenon attributed to the geometric characteristics of the Azimuthally Symmetric coordinate system. This prediction aligns with the observed reality of astrophysical bipolar outflows, which are ubiquitous in the universe. The text concludes by contrasting the field equations of ASTG with those of GR, highlighting the distinct theoretical implications of the derived repulsive force.

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, intense millisecond-long radio signals of extragalactic origin. While their origins remain uncertain, leading theories propose that they originate from young magnetars or colliding neutron stars. These events are expected to produce multi-wavelength signals, including optical light. This chapter details the modeling, simulation, and analysis techniques employed in the conception, development, and refinement of high-power laser architectures. It examines key physical phenomena and their influence on the performance of high-power laser components, including the laser gain medium, pump sources, and optical elements. Furthermore, it explores the optical design strategies for high-power laser cavities, along with the approaches for extracting performance metrics and evaluating the impact of various error sources. The discussion also covers error propagation within the gain medium and optical elements, as well as error amplification mechanisms inherent to high-power pumping. Finally, the text addresses reverse engineering efforts for high-power laser systems, including methods to deduce the specifications of proprietary commercial devices.

While GPT-3 and similar large language models have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in various natural language processing tasks, they lack the ability to integrate non-linguistic inputs. This paper introduces a novel method to incorporate visual data into autoregressive text generation by injecting visual embeddings into the pre-trained parameters of a language model without fine-tuning. Our approach involves injecting these visual representations at multiple layers to assess how model sensitivity varies across depths. Experiments conducted on the Visual Question Answering (VQA) benchmark using GPT-2 reveal that our method substantially enhances performance, raising accuracy from a baseline of 12.5% to 22.1%. Furthermore, we apply this technique to the task of generating captions for images from COCO, showing that the resulting image descriptions are of higher quality than those produced by dedicated vision-language models.

This paper introduces a modified RingCT transaction model that enhances privacy by ensuring that all rings within a transaction are completely anonymous relative to one another. Unlike standard RingCT, our approach decouples the construction of each individual ring, granting signers delegated authority to create them independently. This flexibility allows verifiers to generate the necessary signatures for these groups without involving the transaction's original signer. We demonstrate that this method preserves the security guarantees of the Delegated CT framework. Additionally, we show a practical advantage: because the signature for each pool is pre-computed by the signer and finalized for verification, the method significantly reduces the time required for both signing and verifying.

This study details the development of a luminosity scan technique designed to measure and control the horizontal beam emittance at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The method leverages the fact that the instantaneous luminosity depends exponentially on the instantaneous luminous cross-section, which itself varies with the scan parameter. By performing the scan and analyzing the resulting data, one can extract both the horizontal emittance and the effective beta function at the interaction point. The system's performance was validated through tests using simulated LHC data, and the proposed approach was subsequently employed to benchmark the horizontal emittance during LHC runs in 2016.

Driven by data, this study proposes a cooperative modeling framework that leverages the synergy among multiple data sources. It introduces a new method for learning multi-output regression models capable of jointly analyzing datasets with differing dimensions, volumes, and characteristics. This approach is particularly effective for cooperative tasks where data sources are independent yet interdependent. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through applications in cooperative driver behavior modeling and data-driven fault detection.

We calculate the decay widths for $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$, $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-$, and $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-$, obtaining results of $0.11$ keV, $0.14$ keV, and $0.16$ keV respectively. Training neural networks with quantized weights and activations is a promising strategy to lower the computational costs and energy usage associated with deep learning. However, these quantization constraints often result in a non-convex loss landscape riddled with poor local minima. This study introduces a new method to optimize fully quantized neural networks by employing an annealing scheme that commences with soft, continuous weights and progressively transitions to hard, discrete quantized values. The core of this approach is an optimization algorithm designed to handle constrained soft quantization, which is grounded in an inexact proximal gradient framework capable of operating under limited computational budgets. Theoretically, the paper establishes convergence guarantees for the algorithm, which is proven to yield an $\epsilon$-first-order stationary solution within $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ iterations. Furthermore, the work presents a novel variant of Stochastic Gradient Descent tailored for soft quantization that incorporates momentum. Empirical evaluations on MNIST and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that this proposed algorithm surpasses existing benchmarks in both training speed and final accuracy.

This paper examines the real Jacobi group $ax + by + cz = 0$ and its linear representation on spaces of polynomials. It specifically investigates the decomposition of this representation according to the spaces of homogeneous degree-$k$ polynomials in three variables.

Verifying facts based on a provided table is a challenging task that demands both natural language comprehension and logical reasoning. Although existing models achieve reasonable results, they frequently err due to linguistic ambiguities and logical fallacies. This study investigates decomposition as a strategy to address these issues. By breaking down complex input sentences into multiple simpler sub-claims, the approach enables targeted verification of each claim against the table. Consequently, decomposition clarifies both the natural language structure and the underlying logical assertions. Experiments conducted on the TFact dataset demonstrate that this method yields significant performance gains.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are highly effective for creating realistic synthetic data, yet their non-discriminative nature restricts them to generating data in an unstructured manner. This paper introduces a new GAN architecture that utilizes latent space conditioning to address this limitation, enabling the generation of data in a structured format. We validate this approach on two tasks: the synthesis of images depicting human faces and the creation of synthetic tabular data. Results indicate that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in both areas.

Bayesian nested sampling (BNS) functions as a powerful technique for simultaneous posterior inference and evidence calculation, though its efficacy hinges on the quality of the prior predictive distribution used to sample from. This study provides a comparative analysis of three such sampling methods: MCMC, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC). By examining both synthetic and real-world datasets, we evaluate their performance regarding acceptance rates, computational speed, and the quality of samples generated. Our findings indicate that while MCMC yields the highest acceptance rates, it produces the poorest sample quality and suffers from significant computational inefficiencies. In contrast, both HMC and SMC demonstrate superior overall performance, with SMC emerging as the optimal choice for most applications.

The fault-tolerant distance labeling problem seeks to assign a compact set of distances to each vertex in a graph such that the exact distance between any two nodes can be recovered from the intersection of their respective labeled sets. We present an algorithm that constructs such labels for any simple planar graph with $n$ vertices in $O(n)$ space. Specifically, for any pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, the distance $d(u,v)$ can be computed in $O(n^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ time for any $\varepsilon > 0$. Furthermore, our approach yields a compact set of size $O(n^{1/2+\varepsilon})$ that remains valid even if up to $k$ edges are removed, allowing the query time to degrade only slightly to $O((n+k)^{1/2+\varepsilon})$.

We investigate the time- and frequency-domain two-particle correlations of a two-site Bose-Hubbub model featuring two-site superexchange and drive-dissipate processes. By employing the time evolution of the second quantized density matrix alongside the Fourier transform of the time-delayed correlation function, we map the full second-order correlation function $g^{(2)}$. Our analysis reveals that the resulting frequency and time-domain data are reciprocal, a relationship we confirm using the Hilbert transform. We demonstrate that the second-order correlation function serves as a robust probe for detecting quantum phase transitions and diagnosing nonclassical states. Furthermore, we illustrate that the combined time- and frequency-domain $g^{(2)}$ measurements can uniquely distinguish between various two-particle entangled and non-classical quantum resources.

This paper demonstrates that the semi-group associated with the operator $-A u + b \cdot \nabla u$, where $A$ is an elliptic matrix and the vector field $b \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, generates an analytic contraction on $L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for all $p \in (1, \infty)$. Furthermore, the associated semigroup exhibits ultracontractivity and a smooth pointwise kernel. These findings are significant because they hold even when the symmetric elliptic matrix $A$ lacks sufficient regularity or explicit coercivity.

Recent research has established that Gaussian Process (GP) models are inherently capable of identifying out-of-distribution (OOD) instances. This study introduces a novel approach to leveraging this capability within deep neural networks (DNNs) by integrating GP layers. Unlike previous attempts that relied on heuristic modifications to fit GPs into DNN architectures, our method utilizes a distributional formulation of the GP, ensuring seamless compatibility with standard DNN layers. This framework also accommodates both supervised and unsupervised contexts. Empirical evaluations on synthetic data and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed Distributional Gaussian Process (DG P) layers achieve superior OOD detection performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

This study investigates an open, driven, one-dimensional system of particles within a time-periodically modulated optical lattice, where the driving frequency exhibits a slow linear drift. The system's dynamics are modeled using the time-evolution operator of a Lindblad master equation, which incorporates Floquet-heating-induced particle loss and tunneling suppression due to the periodic drive. Under these conditions, the system stabilizes in a unique "scar-like" non-thermal state. We demonstrate that as the linear drift rate decreases, the system's entropy and energy drop significantly, culminating in Bose condensation. This phenomenon is attributed to the system's non-ergodicity, which prevents heating to infinite temperature. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations employing both the time-evolution operator method and a mean-field approach based on a Lindblad-Gross-Pitaevskii equation.

This paper establishes a uniform Hölder continuity for solutions to the Monge–Ampère equation and strengthens the Alexandrov maximum principle. We demonstrate that any solution $u$ of $\det D^2 u = f$ on a bounded open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, where $f \in L^\infty(\Omega)$ and $0 < \lambda < f < \Lambda < \infty$ almost everywhere, satisfies the estimate:
$$ \sup_{x,y \in \Omega} \frac{|u(x) - u(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha} \leq C, $$
with the exponent $\alpha = \frac{1}{2} \left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{\Lambda}\right)$ and a constant $C$ that depends solely on $n$, $\lambda$, and $\Lambda$. Furthermore, we refine the established bound on second derivatives for such solutions.

Time-domain characterization of non-periodic optical clocks is presented using a stochastic approach. The work focuses on two specific types of non-periodic noise: single noise events and random fluctuations. A general formalism is developed to define a comprehensive set of noise metrics, which are then applied to model the random fluctuations observed in optical lattice clocks. The analysis concludes by evaluating the effectiveness of these time-domain metrics in model discrimination.

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Service Function Chaining (SFC) are increasingly vital for delivering high-performance network services. While SDN centralizes control and SFC orchestrates virtualized services at the network edge to ensure low latency, SFC is highly susceptible to link failures and resource constraints, which can disrupt real-time services. This paper introduces a novel SDN architecture that leverages fog computing to deliver robust failure recovery and mitigation strategies. Our approach employs machine learning to analyze historical failure data and predict future risks, enabling the system to proactively prevent failures by optimizing virtual network function (VNF) placement. Furthermore, the system minimizes energy consumption by adjusting resource allocation dynamically based on current traffic loads. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed solution significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both reliability and energy efficiency.

Overfitting remains a critical challenge in deep learning, prompting the development of numerous regularization techniques. This study employs a recent approach known as "gradient surgery" to systematically analyze the effects of various loss functions. By visualizing gradient landscapes across different datasets, we observe that overfitting arises when the optimization trajectory enters these regions. We demonstrate that the specific impact of a loss function on overfitting is contingent upon the gradient landscape of the data distribution. Furthermore, we identify that certain loss functions can be modified to mitigate overfitting without altering model performance on test data.

We introduce a new class of tensor networks designed to represent approximate holographic quantum error correction codes that exhibit power-law correlations. Our approach extends the standard MERA framework by incorporating hyperbolic tilings of higher dimensions, specifically utilizing $d$-dimensional structures where the original MERA corresponds to the case of $d=2$. We name this construction Hyper-Invariant MERA (HyMERA). By employing a variational strategy, we determine the quantum states for which these networks are valid, identifying them as roughly holographic codes capable of sustaining power-law correlations. Our findings indicate that the networks are not exactly holographic but approximate the geometry of a $((N, k, d_{\text{eff}}))$-qude with an effective code distance $d_{\text{eff}}$ scaling as $O(N^{1/2})$. Consequently, the resulting code distance is lower than that of HyMERA built on $((N, k, d_{\text{eff}}))$-tilings, which would offer an $O(N)$ distance. Despite this reduction, the HyMERA networks with power-law correlations are distinguished by their simplicity and the fact that they can be constructed in polynomial time. Our analysis reveals that the networks can be built in polynomial time, and the resulting code distance is lower than that of HyMERA built on $((N, k, d_{\text{eff}}))$-tilings, which would offer an

This study investigates the spacing between filaments in the Galactic Center (GC) region, utilizing a sample of 100 filaments identified in a prior work. We define filament spacing as the shortest distance from a specific filament to its nearest neighbor. Our analysis reveals that the distribution of these spacacements is non-Gaussian and exhibits a power-law behavior at small scales, transitioning to an exponential falloff at large scales. The spacing distribution is notably dependent on the filament's width; however, when filaments are normalized by their width, the power-law behavior persists up to larger scales. Furthermore, we examine the spatial arrangement of filaments and find that they are not randomly distributed. Instead, they tend to cluster in groups of three or more, with these groups arranged in linear or curved formations.

Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) is a strategy that lowers energy consumption by deliberately decreasing the voltage supplied to consumers. In this paper, we propose and analyze a distributed algorithm for optimal CVR tailored for modern distribution grids equipped with on-load tap changers (OLTCs) and shunt reactive power controllers. The proposed method ensures local decision-making at each OLTC, rendering the approach well-suited for implementation within traditional secondary distribution networks. To validate the stability of the algorithm, we employ the contraction mapping principle. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through simulations on the IEEE 123-bus distribution system, which is integrated with a realistic model of a 12.47/0.48 kV OLTC.

We investigate nonstochastic bandits and scenarios with an arbitrary number of experts, focusing on the impact of varying delay times for each arm or expert. In this environment, the algorithmist selects actions without immediate feedback; instead, both the incurred loss and the revealed expert outcomes are observed after a specific latency period. We demonstrate that standard regret analysis remains applicable, establishing that there exist universal algorithms capable of achieving $\tilde{O}(K^{3/2}D)$ and $\tilde{O}(K^{1/2}KD)$ bounds for bandits and experts respectively, where $K$ represents the number of arms and $D$ the maximum delay. We further prove these bounds are tight up to logarithmic factors. Additionally, we examine a setting where the observation delay is correlated with the chosen action's inherent cost, showing that this dependency creates a fundamental trade-off between minimizing regret and minimizing cumulative cost.

Dialogue systems are increasingly being deployed in real-world scenarios to interact with humans via text. However, current approaches often rely on hand-crafted rules or reinforcement learning, which struggle to produce natural, contextually appropriate, and engaging conversations. This paper introduces a new framework designed to generate human-like dialogue by leveraging large-scale datasets of human-to-human conversations. Our approach learns to create lifelike responses by modeling the joint probability distribution of an entire dialogue, effectively capturing the interplay between a system's utterances and human reactions. To address the computational challenges of training on extensive dialogue data, we introduce a novel variational inference method that enables efficient inference within this conversational framework. Experiments demonstrate that our model generates text that is significantly more human-like than existing alternatives. Furthermore, we show that this framework can be adapted to specific tasks, such as enhancing user engagement or maintaining a particular persona.

This study examines the behavior of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at finite temperature and chemical potential, with a particular focus on the QCD phase diagram. We analyze recent findings from lattice simulations concerning the pseudocritical temperature of chiral symmetry restoration, the chiral condensate, quark number susceptibility, and the crossover transition temperature as functions of the quark mass. Additionally, we explore the potential existence of a critical point within the phase diagram.

The offshore wind turbine industry is increasingly relying on numerical models to forecast loads and assess structural integrity. While computational fluid dynamics (CFD) offers a highly accurate method for simulating loads, its prohibitive computational cost makes it unsuitable for routine design and analysis. To address this, the authors propose a probabilistic surrogate model that combines Gaussian processes (GP) with a multi-fidelity approach. This method constructs a GP-based regression to estimate the discrepancy between CFD and less expensive Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulations. This probabilistic correction is then applied to the RANS outputs to generate improved load estimates. The study demonstrates that this chained GP approach significantly outperforms standard methods, such as using a single low-fidelity simulation or applying a deterministic bias correction.

Natural disasters can be detected and analyzed by examining social media. This study utilizes Twitter data concerning the September 2020 earthquake in Izmir, Turkey, to assess the impact of the event. The analysis employed both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitatively, the researchers calculated the volume of tweets generated by the disaster and compared this figure against the typical daily volume. Qualitative analysis involved a content analysis of tweet text, complemented by a geospatial analysis of tweet locations. The findings indicate that the number of tweets produced during the earthquake was 10.5 times greater than the average daily volume.

A group $G$ is defined as $\mathbb{R}_\infty$ if, for every pair of conjugacy classes in its braid group $G$, there exists a finite index subgroup $G$ contained within that class. This paper demonstrates that the quotient of a generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar group by its lower central series does not possess the $\mathbb{R}_\infty$ property.

We introduce a forward-optimization approach for time-resolved spectroscopy that reconstructs the initial quantum state of a system. This method involves representing the time-evolved wavefunction as a linear combination of a fixed set of trial trajectories and determining the optimal coefficients through optimization. This objective function is designed to maximize the overlap between the simulated time-resolved spectroscopy and the experimentally measured data. We demonstrate that this trajectory-expansion method is highly versatile, applicable to a wide range of spectroscopy techniques, including 2D electronic spectroscopy, time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, and time-resolved X-ray scattering. Furthermore, we show that this expansion offers robustness against noisy experimental data and maintains efficiency when employing a relatively small number of trajectories.

This paper introduces SceNDD, a naturalistic driving dataset designed to enhance the development of autonomous driving systems. The data captures real-world scenarios from a vehicle equipped with a 77GHz radar and a 16-channel lidar, recorded at 25 fps. It encompasses diverse maneuvers such as highway driving, parking, and navigating congested streets. To support rigorous testing, the dataset includes specific drives targeting edge cases like sudden braking, obstacle avoidance, and handling stationary hazards. Additionally, we provide a novel, open-source simulator capable of replicating the exact driving conditions recorded in SceNDD, thereby enabling the evaluation of various algorithms under identical, realistic environments.

Boundary and interface conformal field theories (CFTs) are essential components within the framework of rational conformal field theories, frequently employed to construct consistent conformal string theories. This study investigates the application of reflected entropy within boundary and interface CFTs, demonstrating that the principle of reversed triangle inequality holds for this quantity. Additionally, we establish the existence of a reversed conformal dimension and a reversed central charge specific to these contexts. By leveraging the properties of reversed entropy, we derive constraints on the conformal reversed central charge, thereby offering a novel methodology for analyzing boundary and interface CFTs.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have emerged as a promising technology to boost spectral efficiency in 6G systems. However, implementing RIS in Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) environments presents significant challenges in channel estimation, primarily due to a scarcity of Cyclic Prefix (CP) and the influence of non-ideal hardware components. This paper introduces an Enhanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) framework designed to mitigate these issues. The proposed method employs a two-stage estimation process: first, it uses a deep neural network (DNN) to correct imperfections in RIS hardware, and subsequently, it utilizes the refined data to estimate the channel via the enhanced ELM algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing techniques, delivering superior accuracy and significantly faster computational speeds.

This work examines the deformation theory of G₂-instantons within a nearly G₂ framework. We demonstrate that the standard deformation spaces for G₂-instantons on nearly G₂ manifolds align with those on pure G₂ holonomy manifods, specifically resembling the moduli space defined by the kernel of the linearized Baumin instanton equation modulo gauge transformations. In contrast, on a nearly G₂ holonomy manifold, an additional vector space emerges in this relationship; its construction relies on closed forms that are both self-dual and harmonic.

The widespread adoption of contact tracing applications has been a defining feature of the global response to the COVID-19 pandemic. These tools aim to curb viral transmission by identifying and isolating individuals who have been exposed to the virus. While the primary objective is to mitigate the health crisis, a significant challenge lies in protecting user privacy. This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing the privacy risks of such applications, specifically within the context of the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Susceptible (SISIR) or Susceptible-Infected-Removed-Susceptible (SISIR) model (commonly referred to as SIR or SIS in literature, here adapted to the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Susceptible framework). By examining the uncertainty surrounding user health status, we demonstrate that the privacy of both users and their contacts is contingent upon the application's design parameters. Our findings indicate that anonymity can be compromised when the app's coverage is extensive, the precision of its testing capabilities is high, and the proportion of the population that is infected is substantial.

This article explores the feasibility of quantum processing within the brain, reviewing current research on how neurons might harness quantum effects. We examine the mechanisms by which quantum phenomena could facilitate information processing and storage, alongside the potential role of quantum noise in generating neural variability. Finally, we outline future research directions aimed at clarifying how quantum phenomena influence biological systems.

This work introduces a code generator built in ACL2 capable of producing C programs paired with formal proofs of their functional specifications. The system relies on a shallow embedding of C within ACL2, a foundation also utilized to develop the code generator itself.
